pool.name: seed_check_binary
pool.instruction:
For each reference fact, decide whether the clinical note CAPTURES it - stated verbatim, stated
in different words, or unambiguously implied by what the note does say. A faithful paraphrase, a
correct unit or dose conversion, an accepted abbreviation, and the same fact recorded in an
unexpected section of the note all count as captured. Anything the note simply does not carry, in
any form, is not captured.

Judge only whether each fact is there. Do not judge the note's style, length, ordering or
formatting, and do not penalise it for carrying extra material.

pool.name: v3p-01
pool.instruction:
For each numbered reference fact, judge whether the note conveys the same clinical proposition, not merely whether it contains related words.

First identify the fact’s load-bearing content: the patient/finding/action involved; polarity or negation; timing/currentness; site/laterality; value, dose, route or frequency if relevant; who said or did it when attribution matters; certainty level such as possible/probable/confirmed/ruled out/not established; and any stated reason, red flag, pertinent negative, diagnosis, plan, urgency, or “only/no other” qualifier that changes the clinical meaning.

Mark a fact present when the note carries that load-bearing content explicitly, by faithful paraphrase, by accepted abbreviation, by a conventional clinical phrase, or by an unavoidable implication from a heading or context. It may be in any section and need only be recorded once. Do not require conversational wording, duplicate mentions, exact order, or unnecessary detail. A broad but clinically standard statement can cover a narrower fact when its scope clearly includes it, such as a relevant normal examination phrase, a system-wide negative, or a medication/allergy/status entry under the appropriate heading.

Mark a fact absent when the note does not let a reader recover the load-bearing proposition from the note alone. In particular:
- A mere mention of the same topic, symptom, medication, diagnosis, or plan is not enough if the required relationship is missing.
- A surviving fragment is not enough if the fact depends on the dropped element, such as the working diagnosis, explanatory link, reason for urgency, dose, current medication status, “no other” qualifier, red flag, or pertinent negative.
- If the note states an incompatible version of the fact, mark the reference fact absent: opposite polarity; present vs denied; assessed vs not assessed; different dose/value/timing/site; wrong source or attribution where source matters; or a symptom term used in a different clinical context.
- Preserve certainty. A possible, suspected, differential, working, or to-be-excluded diagnosis is not captured by a note that records it as confirmed; a confirmed diagnosis is not captured by a note that records only a query; “not established” or “not ruled out” is not captured by documenting the finding as absent.
- For medication, contraception, allergy, past history, social history, and occupation facts, require the status the fact asserts. Mentioning an item somewhere else does not by itself establish that it is current, the only medication, absent, denied, or part of the formal medication/allergy/history list unless the note’s wording or section unambiguously does so.
- For patient ideas, concerns, expectations, clinician explanations, counselling, safety-netting, and plans, require the substantive content being attributed, not just that discussion occurred.

Be generous about faithful clinical compression, abbreviations, and section placement, but do not fill in missing qualifiers from medical common sense or from what would usually be true. The question is whether this note actually carries this fact, with its clinically important meaning intact.

pool.name: v3p-02
pool.instruction:
For each numbered reference fact, decide whether the note lets a clinical reader recover that same proposition from the note itself. Judge semantic coverage, not keyword overlap and not overall note quality.

Work fact by fact using this approach:

1. Identify the minimum load-bearing proposition.
   Include the elements that change clinical meaning: the patient/finding/action; polarity or negation; timing/currentness; site/laterality; severity, value, dose, route or frequency when relevant; attribution/source when it matters; certainty level; and any stated diagnosis, differential, reason, explanation, red flag, pertinent negative, “only/no other” qualifier, urgency, safety-net threshold, counselling point, or linked plan.

2. Decide whether the note carries that proposition.
   Mark present when the load-bearing content is stated explicitly, faithfully paraphrased, expressed by accepted abbreviation, captured by a conventional clinical phrase, or unavoidably implied by a heading or local context. The fact may appear in any section and need only appear once.

3. Before marking absent, actively look for faithful compression.
   A clean clinical note may compress conversational detail into standard clinical wording. Do not require exact wording, duplicate mentions, exact ordering, or non-load-bearing colour. A broader conventional statement can cover a narrower fact when its scope clearly includes it, such as a relevant normal-examination phrase, a system-wide negative, or a medication/allergy/status entry under the appropriate heading.

Mark absent only when the load-bearing proposition is not recoverable, is contradicted, or is weakened into a different clinical proposition.

Important distinctions:

- Related topic is not enough. A note can mention the same symptom, medication, diagnosis, investigation, plan, or discussion while omitting the part that makes the reference fact clinically meaningful. If the fact depends on a dropped element, mark absent.

- Composite facts require their linked parts. If a fact says both that something was found and why an action was taken, both the finding and the explanatory link must be recoverable. If a fact says both prior experience and willingness/intention, both must be recoverable. If a fact combines occupation/context with the patient’s ideas, concerns, or lack of explanation, both must be recoverable unless one part is clearly incidental.

- Preserve polarity and certainty. Denied is not the same as present. Possible/suspected/to-be-excluded is not the same as confirmed. Confirmed is not the same as queried. “Not established,” “not assessed,” or “not ruled out” is not the same as documented absent.

- If the note states an incompatible version of the fact, mark the reference fact absent: opposite polarity; different dose/value/timing/site/laterality; wrong current status; wrong attribution where attribution matters; a symptom used in a different context; or a plan, diagnosis, test result, or counselling point that changes the meaning.

Negative process facts and additions:
- Some reference facts assert that something was not done, not performed, not discussed, not advised, not mentioned, or not established in the consultation. For these process/absence-of-discussion facts, a clinical note may conventionally carry the fact by not recording the item in the relevant section.
- If such a fact says a test, examination manoeuvre, diagnosis, counselling point, escalation threshold, or management item was not performed/discussed/advised, mark it present when the note also does not record it.
- Mark it absent if the note records that item as performed, positive/negative, advised, diagnosed, or discussed.
- Do not apply this silence-as-present rule to ordinary clinical negatives such as symptoms denied, allergies denied, no medications, no past history, or no suicidal ideation; those require explicit wording or a conventional negative phrase.

Medication, allergy, contraception, past history, social history, and occupation:
- Require the status asserted by the fact: current, regular, historical, newly prescribed, stopped, changed, advised to avoid, only medication/allergy, no known, or denied.
- A drug name appearing somewhere does not by itself establish current use, prior use, regular use, dose, continuation, discontinuation, or safety advice.
- A prescription or plan to take a medication does not prove the patient was already taking it unless the note uses current-status language such as “currently taking,” “on,” “regular,” “continues,” or “remains on.”
- If the fact is about concomitant medicines, interaction risk, or medication-safety counselling, the note must make that relationship or advice recoverable, not merely list both drug names.
- Allergy facts require the allergy status and any “only/no other/NKDA” qualifier when that qualifier is load-bearing. A medication listed as treatment is not the same as an allergy entry.

Examination, investigations, and referrals:
- If a fact includes a specific examination finding, preserve the clinically meaningful detail such as site, side, grade, character, or whether it is new/incidental when stated.
- A plan for a test or referral does not by itself record the examination finding that justified it unless the note also states the finding or clearly links the test to that finding.
- A generic “for further evaluation” plan is not enough for a fact whose load-bearing content is the reason for the investigation.

Patient ideas, concerns, expectations, explanations, counselling, safety-netting, and shared plans:
- Require the substantive content, not merely that a discussion occurred.
- “Discussed,” “advised,” “safety-netted,” or “counselled” is present only for a general discussion fact. It is absent for a fact requiring specific advice, a specific concern, a specific threshold, or a specific explanation unless that content is recoverable.
- Patient wording may be paraphrased clinically, but do not convert distress, frustration, or figurative language into a different psychiatric or risk assessment. Explicit denial of self-harm or suicidal ideation must not be overridden by a nonspecific expression of not coping.

Use extra material in the note carefully:
- Extra statements do not make unrelated reference facts absent.
- Extra statements do matter when they contradict a reference fact, alter its certainty/status, or violate a reference fact that says something was not done, not discussed, or not advised.

Be generous about faithful clinical compression, accepted abbreviations, conventional section meanings, and reasonable paraphrase. Be strict about load-bearing qualifiers, polarity, certainty, current status, “only/no other” qualifiers, reasons for actions, red flags, pertinent negatives, and substantive counselling or patient-perspective content. Do not fill in missing qualifiers from medical common sense or from what would usually be true; ask whether this note actually carries this fact with its clinically important meaning intact.

pool.name: v3p-03
pool.instruction:
For each numbered reference fact, decide whether the clinical note itself lets a clinical reader recover the same proposition. Judge semantic coverage fact by fact, not keyword overlap, not plausibility from medical background, and not the overall quality of the note.

Your goal is discrimination: mark a fact present when the note truly carries it in faithful clinical wording, and absent when the note only mentions the surrounding topic while dropping or changing the clinically meaningful part.

Use this method for every fact:

1. Identify the minimum load-bearing proposition.

   Ask what must be true for the reference fact to have been documented correctly. Include every element that changes clinical meaning, such as:
   - patient, symptom, sign, diagnosis, medication, test, referral, advice, or plan;
   - polarity/negation;
   - current versus past status;
   - timing, duration, frequency, dose, value, grade, severity, route, or quantity when clinically meaningful;
   - site, side, distribution, character, or specific body system;
   - certainty level: confirmed, suspected, possible, excluded, queried, to be ruled out;
   - attribution/source when it matters, including patient-reported concern versus clinician assessment;
   - “only,” “no other,” “rather than,” “not due to,” “instead,” or other contrast/limiting qualifiers;
   - pertinent negatives and red flags;
   - the reason, indication, explanation, or causal link for an investigation, treatment, referral, or urgency;
   - the substantive content of counselling, safety-netting, shared decision-making, or patient ideas/concerns/expectations.

   Do not treat every word in the reference fact as equally important. Conversational colour, repeated mentions, exact ordering, and minor wording differences need not be preserved. But if a detail would change diagnosis, risk, urgency, management, interpretation, or the reason for a plan, it is load-bearing.

2. Decide whether the note carries that proposition.

   Mark present when the load-bearing content is explicitly stated, faithfully paraphrased, expressed by an accepted clinical abbreviation, captured by conventional clinical wording, or unavoidably implied by a heading or local context.

   The fact may appear in any section and only needs to appear once. A clean note may compress speech into clinical language, combine overlapping facts, or record a normal/negative finding using standard phrasing.

   Examples of acceptable coverage in principle:
   - accepted abbreviations and synonyms, such as SOB/dyspnoea, HTN/hypertension, MI/heart attack, VTE/venous thromboembolism;
   - conventional normal examination phrases, when their scope clearly includes the finding required by the fact;
   - medication/allergy/status entries under the appropriate heading, when they carry the required current/past/no-known status;
   - a broader system-wide negative, when it unambiguously includes the narrower negative and does not lose a required qualifier.

3. Before marking absent, actively look for faithful compression.

   Prefer present when the same clinical proposition is recoverable despite different wording. Do not require:
   - exact wording from the reference fact;
   - duplicate documentation of something already recorded once;
   - the same section or order;
   - lay wording if clinical wording is equivalent;
   - incidental details that do not affect the clinical meaning of the fact.

   However, do not use “compression” to supply a missing load-bearing element. A topic mention is not enough if the fact depends on a specific dropped detail, contrast, reason, risk factor, red flag, or advice threshold.

Mark absent when the load-bearing proposition is not recoverable from the note, is contradicted, or is weakened into a different clinical proposition.

Important distinctions:

- Related topic is not enough.
  A note may mention the same symptom, sign, medication, diagnosis, investigation, referral, or discussion but still omit the part that makes the reference fact clinically meaningful. If the fact requires a specific feature, qualifier, explanation, or link, that feature must be recoverable.

- Partial surviving mentions require special scrutiny.
  If the note contains only a generic surviving phrase, ask whether it preserves the exact proposition or merely names the topic.
  - “Pain with movement” does not by itself document preserved ability/range of movement.
  - “Numbness/tingling” does not by itself document weakness, loss of power, or a clinician’s conclusion of weakness.
  - “Murmur” does not by itself document grade, location, newness, incidental nature, or the reason an investigation was ordered unless those parts are also stated or clearly linked.
  - “Discussed risks,” “safety-netted,” “for further evaluation,” or “suitable for treatment” does not by itself document the specific risk, threshold, reason, or contraindication named in the fact.

- Composite facts require their linked parts.
  If a fact says both that something was found and why an action was taken, both the finding and the explanatory link must be recoverable.
  If a fact combines patient experience with willingness, intention, concern, expectation, or clinician interpretation, both parts must be recoverable unless one is clearly incidental.
  If a fact contains a contrast such as “rather than,” “not,” “instead,” or “no other,” preserve that contrast.

- Preserve polarity and certainty.
  Denied is not the same as present.
  Possible/suspected/to-be-excluded is not the same as confirmed.
  Confirmed is not the same as queried.
  “Not established,” “not assessed,” or “not ruled out” is not the same as documented absent.
  If the note states an incompatible version of the fact, mark the reference fact absent.

- Do not infer missing facts from clinical common sense.
  A plan, diagnosis, or treatment may make a missing fact plausible, but plausibility is not documentation. The note must carry the fact itself or an unambiguous equivalent.

Negative process facts and additions:

- Some reference facts assert that something was not done, not performed, not discussed, not advised, not mentioned, or not established in the consultation.
- For these process/absence-of-discussion facts, a clinical note may conventionally carry the fact by not recording the item in the relevant section.
- Mark such a fact present when the note also does not record that test, examination manoeuvre, diagnosis, counselling point, escalation threshold, or management item.
- Mark it absent if the note records the item as performed, advised, diagnosed, discussed, positive, negative, or planned.
- This includes fabricated or extra safety-netting/advice: if the reference fact says particular return advice, escalation advice, counselling, or discussion did not occur, but the note says it did occur, mark the reference fact absent.
- Do not apply silence-as-present to ordinary clinical negatives such as symptoms denied, allergies denied, no medications, no past history, no suicidal ideation, no red flags, or no risk factors. Those require explicit wording or a conventional negative phrase.

Medication, allergy, contraception, past history, social history, and occupation:

- Require the status asserted by the fact: current, regular, historical, newly prescribed, stopped, changed, advised to avoid, no known, denied, only medication/allergy, no other medications/allergies, or relevant family/social context.
- A drug name appearing somewhere does not by itself establish current use, prior use, regular use, dose, continuation, discontinuation, or safety advice.
- A prescription or plan to take a medication does not prove the patient was already taking it unless the note uses current-status language such as “currently taking,” “on,” “regular,” “continues,” or “remains on.”
- If the fact is about concomitant medicines, interaction risk, contraindication screening, or medication-safety counselling, the note must make that relationship, risk, or advice recoverable, not merely list the items separately.
- Allergy facts require allergy status and any “only/no other/NKDA” qualifier when that qualifier is load-bearing. A medication listed as treatment is not the same as an allergy entry.

Risk factors, contraindications, and family history:

- A final assessment such as “low risk,” “suitable,” “no contraindications,” or “risk factors reviewed” does not by itself document each specific risk factor or negative named in the fact.
- If a fact names a specific contraindication or risk factor, the note must record that specific factor or a standard unambiguous equivalent.
- Accepted clinical umbrella terms can cover their standard components when truly equivalent, such as “no VTE” covering no history of DVT/PE.
- Be cautious with vague umbrella wording. A broad phrase such as “no relevant history,” “no clotting issues,” or “no clot history” may show the general topic was considered, but it does not necessarily preserve a fact requiring a specific previous diagnosis, anatomical event, or named condition unless the local wording makes the equivalence unmistakable.
- Family history facts require the relevant condition and the correct polarity/relative when stated. A different cancer, different relative, or positive versus negative family history changes the proposition.

Examination, investigations, and referrals:

- If a fact includes a specific examination finding, preserve clinically meaningful detail such as site, side, grade, character, severity, range, distribution, whether it is new, whether it is incidental, and whether it is positive or negative.
- A plan for a test or referral does not by itself record the examination finding that justified it unless the note states the finding or clearly links the test/referral to that finding.
- A generic phrase such as “for further evaluation,” “to investigate,” or “routine referral” is not enough for a fact whose load-bearing content is the specific reason, urgency, red flag, or abnormal finding.
- Conversely, if the fact only requires that a test/referral was planned for a broadly stated problem, a faithful broad plan may be sufficient.

Symptoms, function, and neurological content:

- Distinguish sensory symptoms from motor symptoms.
  Numbness, tingling, paraesthesia, altered sensation, or loss of feeling are not the same as weakness, loss of power, reduced strength, clumsiness, or objective motor deficit unless the note explicitly links them.
- Distinguish pain provoked by movement from preserved or reduced movement.
  A statement that movement worsens pain does not by itself say how much movement the patient can perform.
- Distinguish functional limitation caused by pain from neurological loss of function, unless the note makes that attribution clear.
- If the fact says the clinician concluded or assessed something, patient symptoms alone do not cover it unless the clinician assessment is documented or unavoidably implied.

Patient ideas, concerns, expectations, explanations, counselling, safety-netting, and shared plans:

- Require the substantive content, not merely that a discussion occurred.
- “Discussed,” “advised,” “counselled,” “reassured,” “safety-netted,” or “return precautions given” is present only for a general discussion fact.
- It is absent for a fact requiring specific advice, a specific concern, a specific threshold, a specific explanation, a specific risk/benefit, or a specific agreed plan unless that content is recoverable.
- Patient wording may be paraphrased clinically, but do not convert distress, frustration, or figurative language into a different psychiatric or risk assessment.
- Explicit denial of self-harm or suicidal ideation must not be overridden by a nonspecific expression of not coping.

Handling contradictions and extra material:

- Extra statements do not make unrelated reference facts absent.
- Extra statements do matter when they contradict the reference fact, alter its polarity/certainty/status, or violate a reference fact that says something was not done, discussed, advised, or established.
- If the note contains both a correct version and an incompatible version of the same load-bearing fact, mark absent unless the correct version is clearly the operative documented conclusion and the incompatible wording is plainly irrelevant or superseded.

Final calibration:

Be generous about faithful clinical compression, conventional section meanings, accepted abbreviations, and reasonable paraphrase. This avoids falsely penalising complete notes.

Be strict about load-bearing qualifiers, polarity, certainty, current/past status, specific risk factors, “only/no other” qualifiers, reasons for actions, red flags, pertinent negatives, and substantive counselling or patient-perspective content. This avoids giving credit for partial topic mentions that have lost the clinically important proposition.

When uncertain, ask: “Could a clinical reader recover this exact clinically meaningful fact from the note itself, without already knowing the consultation?” If yes, mark present. If the reader could only infer that the general topic was mentioned, mark absent.

pool.name: v3p-04
v3p-05
v3p-06
pool.instruction:
For each numbered reference fact, decide whether the note lets a clinical reader recover the same clinically meaningful proposition from the note itself. Judge semantic coverage, not keyword overlap, wording style, or overall note quality.

Your aim is precise discrimination. Mark present for faithful clinical paraphrase or compression. Mark absent when the note genuinely omits, contradicts, weakens, or changes a load-bearing part of the reference fact, even if it mentions the same general topic.

Decision approach:

1. Identify the minimum load-bearing proposition.
   Ask what must be true for the fact to be clinically preserved. Load-bearing elements include:
   - patient/finding/action;
   - polarity or negation;
   - timing, currentness, sequence, resolution, or recurrence;
   - site/laterality;
   - severity, value, dose, route, frequency, duration, quantity, trend, or oxygen/room-air context when clinically relevant;
   - certainty level, such as possible, suspected, likely, confirmed, excluded, or not present today;
   - source or attribution when it matters;
   - diagnosis, differential, cause, trigger, explanation, rationale, reason for an action, red flag, pertinent negative, “only/no other” qualifier, urgency, safety-net threshold, counselling point, patient concern, expectation, or agreed plan.

   Treat conversational colour, illustrative wording, duplicate mentions, and non-clinical phrasing as non-load-bearing unless the reference fact makes them clinically meaningful.

2. Search the whole note for faithful coverage.
   Mark present when the proposition is explicitly stated, faithfully paraphrased, expressed by accepted abbreviation or clinical shorthand, captured by a conventional heading/section meaning, or unavoidably implied by the local clinical context. The fact may appear anywhere and need only appear once.

   Be generous with ordinary clinical compression:
   - accepted abbreviations such as SOB, CP, NKDA;
   - conventional exam phrases such as “abdo SNT” or “no focal neurology”;
   - relevant system-wide negatives or normal-exam statements that clearly include narrower normal findings;
   - “now asymptomatic” or “symptom-free” covering absence of relevant current symptoms;
   - a broad conventional diagnosis/impression phrase covering a lay equivalent when no extra cause, certainty, or qualifier is required.

   Do not require exact words, exact order, repeated mentions, or lay phrasing if the same clinical meaning is recoverable.

3. Be strict about load-bearing omissions and alterations.
   Mark absent when the note mentions the same symptom, diagnosis, medication, test, plan, or discussion but drops or changes the clinically important part of the fact.

   In particular:
   - Preserve polarity. “No acute asthma attack today” is the opposite of “acute asthma attack today.” A chronic condition or poor control does not imply an acute exacerbation, and an acute event does not imply its absence.
   - Preserve certainty. Possible/suspected/to be excluded is not confirmed; confirmed is not merely queried.
   - Preserve current status. Historical, resolved, current, planned, newly prescribed, continued, stopped, and already taking are distinct when relevant.
   - Preserve timing, sequence, duration, and resolution when they matter, such as an aura lasting about 20 minutes, resolving completely, and doing so before headache onset.
   - Preserve values and measurement context. A generic respiratory or normal-exam statement does not carry a specific observation such as oxygen saturation 94% on room air.
   - Preserve site, side, dose, route, frequency, duration, value, grade, character, or trend when clinically meaningful.
   - Preserve attribution/source when it matters.
   - Preserve stated reasons and rationales. A medication being continued is not the same as being continued partly for renal benefit unless that rationale is recoverable.
   - Preserve causal attributions and mechanisms. Extra unsupported wording such as syncope or a fall caused by heart failure changes a fall-history fact if the reference fact requires a different or more neutral mechanism.
   - Do not fill missing qualifiers from medical common sense or from what would usually be true.

4. Composite facts require their linked parts.
   If a fact contains both an item and its explanation, both must be recoverable. If it contains both a finding and the action it prompted, both the finding and explanatory link must be recoverable. If it contains prior experience plus willingness/intention, both must be recoverable. If it combines a diagnosis with causes and exclusions, preserve those components.

   For example, a working impression of poor asthma control likely due to poor preventer adherence and poor inhaler technique, with no acute exacerbation, requires the poor-control impression, the adherence/technique rationale, and the no-acute-exacerbation qualifier. A generic asthma label or inhaler plan is not enough.

5. Medication, allergy, contraception, past history, social history, and occupation.
   Require the status asserted by the fact:
   - current use;
   - regular use;
   - intermittent/PRN use;
   - historical use;
   - newly prescribed;
   - stopped;
   - changed;
   - continued;
   - advised to avoid;
   - only medication/allergy;
   - no known/denied;
   - occupation or social context.

   A drug name appearing somewhere does not by itself establish current use, prior use, regularity, dose, continuation, discontinuation, concomitant use, interaction risk, or safety advice. A prescription or plan to take a medication does not prove the patient was already taking it unless the note uses current-status language such as “on,” “currently taking,” “regular,” “continues,” or “remains on.”

   If the fact is about concomitant medicines, interaction risk, avoiding combination therapy, medication-safety counselling, or a reason for continuing/stopping a drug, the note must make that relationship, advice, or rationale recoverable. Allergy facts require allergy status and any “only/no other/NKDA” qualifier when asserted.

6. Diagnosis, impression, differential, and explanation.
   Diagnosis labels, impressions, differentials, explanations, and reassurance are not interchangeable unless they express the same clinical proposition.
   - “Likely,” “suggestive of,” “consistent with,” and “working impression” may be equivalent when they convey the same tentative judgement.
   - Lay and clinical labels may be equivalent when clearly referring to the same condition.
   - If the fact requires a cause or trigger, such as adherence, inhaler technique, food exposure, stress, exertion, trauma, medication effect, infection source, syncope, or heart failure, that cause or trigger must be stated or clearly linked.
   - Reassurance that a serious diagnosis is less likely does not by itself record the positive working diagnosis.
   - “Rule out X” or testing/referral for possible X is not diagnosed X.

7. Examination, investigations, observations, and referrals.
   Preserve specific results and clinically meaningful detail: side, site, character, grade, value, abnormality, normality, whether new/incidental, comparison, and measurement conditions such as “on room air.”
   A plan for a test or referral does not by itself record the finding or reasoning that justified it unless the note states or clearly links that reason. Generic wording such as “bloods arranged,” “ECG done,” “referred,” or “for further assessment” is not enough for a fact requiring a specific result, abnormal finding, or reason.

8. Symptoms and current clinical state.
   Preserve timing and resolution.
   - “Now asymptomatic” or equivalent can cover absence of relevant current symptoms.
   - “No chest pain now” covers no current chest pain, but not necessarily no breathlessness, palpitations, nausea, dizziness, or all symptoms unless the fact only requires chest pain.
   - A historical symptom description does not establish current symptoms unless currentness is clear.
   - A current symptom description does not preserve earlier onset, trigger, duration, progression, sequence, or complete resolution if those are load-bearing.

9. Patient ideas, concerns, expectations, counselling, safety-netting, and shared plans.
   Require the substantive content when the fact specifies it.
   - “Discussed,” “advised,” “counselled,” “reassured,” or “safety-netted” covers only a general discussion fact.
   - It does not cover a specific explanation, concern, preference, advice, contingency, time threshold, or urgent-care instruction unless that content is recoverable.
   - Advice to call 999 for visual loss not clearing within an hour requires both the emergency action and the visual-loss/time threshold.
   - Advice to message/contact the clinician if pain is not improving requires the interim contact action and the non-improvement contingency.
   - A shared plan must preserve the patient-facing action and any important contingency.

   Patient wording may be paraphrased clinically, but do not convert distress, frustration, or figurative language into a different psychiatric or risk assessment. Explicit denial of self-harm, suicidal ideation, plan, or intent must not be overridden by nonspecific statements about not coping.

10. Risk and self-harm facts.
   Preserve the difference between passive thoughts, active thoughts, plan, intent, preparation, attempt, acted behaviour, current risk, historical/recent risk, single episode, recurrent/persistent thoughts, fleeting thoughts, protective steps, and absence of protective steps. If timing, method, setting, non-action, return to safety, lack of plan, or lack of intent is stated, treat it as load-bearing unless clearly incidental.

11. Negative process facts and absence-of-discussion facts.
   Some reference facts assert that something was not done, not performed, not discussed, not advised, not mentioned, or not established in the consultation. For these process facts only, a clinical note may conventionally carry the fact by also not recording that item.
   - If the fact says a test, examination manoeuvre, diagnosis, counselling point, escalation threshold, or management item was not performed/discussed/advised, mark present when the note also does not record it.
   - Mark absent if the note records that item as performed, positive/negative, advised, diagnosed, or discussed.
   - Do not use this silence-as-present rule for ordinary clinical negatives such as denied symptoms, no allergies, no medications, no past history, no alcohol use, no smoking, or no suicidal ideation. Those require explicit wording or a conventional negative phrase.

12. Extra material in the note.
   Extra information does not make unrelated reference facts absent. It matters when it contradicts the reference fact, changes its polarity, certainty, status, timing, cause, mechanism, or attribution, or violates a fact saying something was not done, discussed, diagnosed, or advised.

Final tie-break:
Mark present if the note contains a faithful clinical compression and any missing detail is not load-bearing. Mark absent if a load-bearing qualifier, relationship, rationale, cause, currentness, value, timing, sequence, safety threshold, red flag, pertinent negative, patient-perspective detail, or risk detail is not recoverable from the note itself.

pool.name: v3p-07
pool.instruction:
For each reference fact, decide whether the clinical note carries the same clinical information, not whether it uses the same wording or puts it in the expected section.

Use this approach:

1. Identify the fact’s load-bearing content.
   Ask what would matter clinically if it were omitted or changed. This often includes:
   - diagnosis, assessment, or working impression
   - symptom presence or absence
   - pertinent negatives and explicit denials
   - timing, onset, duration, sequence, or “before/after” relationships
   - laterality, severity, frequency, progression, or functional limitation
   - medication name, dose, route, frequency, duration, PRN/“up to” versus regular use, and maximum dose
   - investigations, follow-up, safety-netting, escalation, or urgency
   - the reason for a plan, referral, test, or level of concern
   - patient preference, agreement, willingness, refusal, prior experience, or “never tried before”
   - an explicit decision not to do something, such as no antibiotic, no admission, no imaging, no referral, or no medication change

2. Mark the fact present when the note states that load-bearing content directly, states it in a clinically equivalent way, or makes it unavoidable from what is written.
   Count as present:
   - faithful paraphrase
   - standard abbreviations and conventional clinical shorthand
   - equivalent medical terminology
   - accepted normal-exam or negative-review phrasing
   - reasonable compression of repeated or overlapping facts
   - the fact appearing in any section of the note
   - a broader statement that clearly includes the specific fact without changing its meaning

3. Mark the fact absent when the note does not carry the load-bearing content.
   This includes cases where the note mentions the same general topic but drops or changes the clinically important part. A topic mention is not enough if the reference fact requires a specific assertion, qualifier, relationship, or decision.

   Common partial-coverage traps:
   - Mentioning a symptom without the required timing, progression, severity, laterality, or functional effect.
   - Mentioning pain with movement without documenting preserved or limited ability to move, if ability is part of the fact.
   - Mentioning conservative or symptomatic management without documenting an explicit “not needed / not indicated / not given” decision, if that decision is the fact.
   - Mentioning a previous absence of treatment without documenting current willingness, refusal, preference, or plan, if that is part of the fact.
   - Mentioning a condition in a problem list or review of systems without the required history context, reason for concern, or causal/temporal relationship.
   - Giving a medication instruction that changes PRN to regular use, changes “up to” into a fixed schedule, invents a dose strength, omits a maximum, or otherwise alters the instruction.
   - Replacing a denial or pertinent negative with a positive statement, uncertainty, or silence.

4. Contradiction or alteration means absent.
   If the note says something incompatible with the reference fact, do not give credit merely because related words appear. A wrong dose, wrong polarity, wrong timing, wrong plan, or wrong patient preference is not a paraphrase.

5. Do not be stricter than the reference fact.
   Do not require conversational detail, exact quotes, repeated mentions, exact section placement, or every minor modifier unless it changes the clinical meaning of the fact. If the note’s wording would allow a clinician to recover the same clinical point without guessing, mark it present.

6. Extra material does not by itself make a reference fact absent.
   Penalize extra or fabricated content only when it contradicts, replaces, weakens, or changes the reference fact being judged.

7. If a reference item is duplicate, overlapping, or more granular than a normal clinical note, mark it present when the note contains a clinically equivalent summary. If an item contains no substantive checkable assertion, treat it as present.
